title: Structural Patterns: Wrapping and Composing Objects
oneLiner: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy and Composite: five ways to put one object in front of, around or inside another.
keyTakeaway: Three of these patterns look identical in code: a class that holds another object and forwards calls to it. Tell them apart by intent. An Adapter changes the interface, a Decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior, and a Proxy keeps the interface and controls access. Facade simplifies many objects into one, and Composite lets one object and a tree of them be treated the same way.
explanation:
Structural patterns are about how classes and objects are assembled into bigger structures. Almost all of them rely on composition (an object holding a reference to another object) rather than inheritance, which is why they are flexible: you can wrap, swap or stack them at runtime.

This family is where interview questions most often turn into "what is the difference between" questions, because Adapter, Decorator and Proxy share the same shape. Read the "often confused with" note under each one, then test yourself in the recognition quiz at the end of the track.

Pick a pattern. Each one shows the intent, when to use it and when not to, a small structure diagram, idiomatic C#, a real .NET example (the Stream classes alone contain three of these five) and the interview angle.
